title: LangChain Project 10: Build a Self-Correcting AI (Guardrails + Auto-Fix Pipeline) | Llama 3 + LCEL
description:
Most AI apps fail in production for one reason: they don’t check themselves. 
They generate an answer… and ship it. 

So in Episode 10 of the LangChain Builder Series, we build a fully local Self-Correcting AI Guardrails System that can: 

✅ Generate an answer 
✅ Evaluate it against clear quality criteria 
✅ Automatically repair mistakes 
✅ Show every step transparently in the UI 

No API keys. No cloud processing. No paid models. 
Everything runs 100% locally using Llama 3 via Ollama, powered by LangChain + LCEL + Streamlit. 

What you’ll build + learn in this episode: 
✔ A clean 3-stage pipeline: Generate → Evaluate → Repair 
✔ Evaluation criteria to detect incomplete, inaccurate, or low-quality answers 
✔ A repair prompt that upgrades, fixes, and refines model output 
✔ How to wire LCEL components into a reusable Guardrails workflow 
✔ A Streamlit UI that visualizes each step (full transparency + debugging) 
✔ How to build safer, smarter responses using only local models — fully offline 

By the end, you’ll have a working self-evaluating AI system that improves its own outputs automatically — a foundational skill for reliable agents, automation pipelines, and production-grade LLM apps. 

Episode 11 goes deeper into reasoning, quality control, and long-form evaluation. 

TIMESTAMPS
00:00 Why AI needs guardrails in production 
00:35 What we’re building: self-correcting local AI 
01:20 The stack: LangChain + LCEL + Streamlit + Llama 3 (Ollama) 
02:10 Designing the 3-stage flow (Generate → Evaluate → Repair) 
03:25 Writing evaluation criteria (what “good” looks like) 
04:40 Building the evaluator chain in LCEL 
05:45 Designing the repair prompt (fix + upgrade output) 
06:55 Wiring evaluator → repair into a reusable guardrails workflow 
08:05 Streamlit UI: show each step + debug the pipeline 
09:10 Testing failure cases (incomplete, wrong, messy formatting) 
10:20 Practical use cases (agents, automations, production tools) 
11:10 What’s next: deeper evaluation + long-form QC (EP12) 
11:35 Subscribe + comment what to evaluate first

Want to build agents and AI tools that are reliable enough for real workflows — not just demos?

transcript.text: [music]
All right. Hey everyone, welcome back to
the lang chain by project series. And
today we're building something that
feels genuinely smart. An AI that
doesn't just answer your question. It
actually checks its own answer, judges
the quality, and fixes itself if it's
wrong.
This is one of those projects where you
immediately understand the power of
Langchain. You ask a question, the AI
responds. Another part of the AI reviews
the response. And if it fails the check,
a third step improves it automatically.
All three steps, generation, evaluation,
and repair, run right on your laptop
through Llama and Streamlit. So, let's
jump straight into the code and see how
this entire self-correcting system is
built. We start with the imports. We
import Streamlit because that's the UI
layer. We import optional from typing
for a helper function later. Then we
bring in chat Olama from the lang chain
community package. This is what connects
us to the local llama model running in
Olama. We also import chat prompt
template to build prompts and stream
output parser to convert the model's
responses into plain text.
Next, we define the model name. Here we
are using Llama 3.23B.
This must match a model that already
exists in your Olama installation.
Then we configure the streamlit page
with a title and a wide layout. After
that, we set up the model. We create the
LLM object using chatma passing the
model name and a temperature of 0.4.
Lower temperature means cleaner, more
controlled answers.
We also create the parser object using
stream output parser which converts the
output into simple text.
Now we create the prompts for the three
stages of our pipeline. The first one is
the generation prompt. This prompt tells
the AI to be helpful, answer clearly and
respond to whatever input the user
provides. It has one placeholder called
input where the user's question will go.
The second prompt is the evaluation
prompt. This part of the AI acts like a
reviewer. We give it the original
question and the AI's answer. Then we
ask it to judge the answer on
correctness, clarity, and completeness.
And most importantly, it must reply in a
fixed format. It either says pass
followed by a short explanation or fail
followed by what is wrong and why. This
strict format is important because the
rest of the pipeline depends on it.
The third prompt is the repair prompt.
This one only runs if the evaluation
step fails. It gets the original
question, the incorrect response, and
the reviewer's feedback. and its job is
simple. Rewrite the answer so it becomes
correct, clear, and complete.
Once the prompts are ready, we turn each
one into a chain by piping the prompt
into the model and then into the parser.
So, we end up with a generation chain,
an evaluation chain, and a repair chain.
Next, we define a small helper function
called get text. This function makes
sure that no matter what shape the model
returns, whether it returns an object or
just a string, we extract clean text
from it. It checks if the response has a
content attribute. If it does, we return
that content. If not, we convert the
entire object to text. This keeps
everything safe and predictable.
Then we create the sidebar. The sidebar
has a title that says guardrail
controls. It has a checkbox that lets
the user choose whether the system
should automatically repair failed
answers. By default, auto repair is
turned on.
Below that, we show a small info box
explaining that this episode
demonstrates self- evaluation,
guardrails, and conditional repair, all
running locally.
Now we move to the main interface. We
set the main title to episode 11
self-correcting AI system.
Then we add a caption that shows the
pipeline in simple words generation
evaluation repair.
Below that we add a horizontal line.
Then we add a text area where the user
can type any question they want. And
finally we add a button called run AI
pipeline.
Now for the execution section. When the
user clicks the run button we first
check if the input text is empty. If it
is we show a warning. If not we begin
the three-step process. Step one is the
generation step. Inside a loading
spinner. We call the generation chain
with the user's input. We extract the
clean text using our get text helper.
Then we display it under a heading
called initial response.
Step two is evaluation.
We show another spinner. Run the
evaluation chain by passing the question
and the answer and extract the feedback.
We display the feedback under evaluation
result. The first line of that feedback
will either be the word pass or the word
fail. We store that first line in a
variable called verdict. If the verdict
is fail and the auto repair checkbox is
enabled, we run the repair step. Inside
a spinner, we call the repair chain
passing the original question, the
incorrect response and the reviewer
feedback. We extract the text and
display it under repaired response.
If the verdict is fail but auto repair
is turned off, we simply show a warning
saying that the response failed review
but repair is disabled.
If the word it is pass then everything
is good and we show a success message
saying the response passed quality
checks.
Finally, at the bottom of the page, we
show a footer that says episode 11 lang
chain lce guardrails.
And that completes the full walkthrough
of the code exactly as it's written.
>> [music]
